Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
• 40-year-old male with 3-day history of acute watery diarrhoea (4–5 × / day), mild abdominal pain, one episode of vomiting, possible low-grade fever, able to maintain oral intake, no blood/mucus, no recent travel or high-risk food exposure.  
• No clinical signs of dehydration on video assessment.  
• Past history notable for asthma; regular use of inhaler called “Laxepro” (name unclear—may not be standard asthma therapy; consider medication reconciliation).  
• Family history significant for colorectal cancer (father age 62).  

Plan (per transcript)  
– Reassurance that presentation most consistent with self-limiting infective gastroenteritis.  
– Hydration advice: maintain high oral fluid intake; start oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) as needed.  
– Dietary advice: “soft diet” (crackers, toast, mashed vegetables); avoid meat, eggs, fish, dairy until 48 h diarrhoea-free; yoghurt permitted for probiotic benefit.  
– Red-flag advice: seek review if diarrhoea ≥ 6–8 episodes/day, signs of dehydration, persistence > 7 days, or appearance of blood/mucus.  
– If persistence or blood, arrange stool sample for culture and possible antibiotics; consider hospital assessment for dehydration if frequency increases.  
– Patient directed to review written advice in app; follow-up PRN.

- management_plan_main: as above (hydration, diet modification, OTC oral rehydration, safety-net, possible stool culture).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood: abrupt onset, watery stools, mild systemic symptoms, self-limiting pattern, no blood.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis – Moderate likelihood: similar presentation though no clear food/travel trigger identified.  
3. Medication-induced diarrhoea (possible SSRI “Lexapro”) – Low–moderate likelihood: patient reports regular “Laxepro,” but unclear if this is escitalopram; symptom cluster favors infection.  (Medication identity conflict noted.)
